title: Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame?
description: After wildfires caused more damage in France this year than at any time since World War Two, many are left asking a single question: why?A major drive
body: After wildfires caused more damage in France this year than at any time since World War Two, many are left asking a single question: why?A major driver is that climate is changing as a result of the well-documented way humanity is burning fossil fuels. Temperatures are only rising.But with records showing that nine out of 10 French wildfires are started by humans, the government in Paris is trying to attribute blame - although it is itself accused of being underprepared for the infernos that have now scorched more than 300,000 acres this summer.The interior ministry has announced 420 arrests of people alleged to have either started the fires deliberately or by accident. Among them are 166 minors.In one case, a 23-year-old man has been accused of deliberately starting 10 fires in the space of five days in the south-eastern Var area last month. He faces 15 years in prison and a €150,000 (£128,000) fine, if convicted.Many others have been tried and immediately sentenced, such as a man who received a three-year jail sentence for starting three recent fires in the Raon-L'Étape forest in the Vosges region. "Only a few square metres of vegetation went up in smoke," noted L'Est Républicain, the newspaper that reported the story.Other prosecutions have been perceived as heavy-handed and unjust. A homeless man and someone with severe autism have reportedly been handed jail terms for throwing cigarette butts."I was amazed at the number of arrests, it feels excessive," admits Muriel Gestas, a lawyer who has represented several people accused of arson, including two firefighters. She doubts many will lead to a conviction.The newspaper Le Monde is also unconvinced. It questions to what extent police have examined these cases, given the short time frame.The authorities' silence on the details - the specific charges, notably whether they involve intent and how the numbers compare with past seasons - rules out any meaningful comparison with previous years, it argues.But Bordeaux prosecutor Renaud Gaudeul told Le Monde that a tough approach was justified by current circumstances. "The conditions for a charge of endangering lives are met for those who throw a cigarette butt or light a barbecue in wooded areas. It only takes a tiny spark for it to start," the newspaper quoted him as saying. Working out how a fire started is, unsurprisingly, not easy."In periods of drought such as this one, all you need is a simple lighter," explains Eric Dufayet, an officer who investigates fires.Once a fire is out, Eric's first task is to map its outline along the edge of the burnt vegetation, then trace it back to its point of origin. If the wind has been steady, that outline often forms a "V" shape. From there, his team works backwards along the path the flames took."If someone deliberately starts a fire, they may not have used only one device," he says. It improves the chances of a DNA or fingerprint sample being found.Experts believe arson accounts for only a small fraction of fires. Most are believed to be accidental, with sparks potentially coming from construction work, faulty electrical equipment, cigarette butts and barbecues."With cigarettes, it's called the '30' rule," says Eric Dufayet. To start a fire, he explains, there must be "a temperature of at least 30C (86F), a maximum of 30% humidity, wind of less than 30km/h (19mph), and at least 30% of the cigarette unburnt."In the current drought, he says it is even easier. If those conditions are met, a fire can easily spread, and fast.According to Michel Lejoyeux, a professor of psychiatry and addictive behaviour at Paris 7 University, people who start fires fall into three categories: those who are careless, those who benefit - with an insurance payout, for example - and pyromaniacs."The pyromaniac doesn't get money, has no spirit of revenge, has no utility of the fire, but he likes the fire," he says.However, pyromania is a rare psychiatric disorder that Lejoyeux says is very difficult to diagnose, and accounts for few arson convictions.Lawyer Muriel Gestas, who has handled several such cases, says some firefighters alleged to have started fires may have wanted to be seen as saviours. For others - notably volunteers earning tax-free overtime - the motive may be financial.Amid concerns over how officials are pursuing suspects, broader worries about wildfires are far from abating. Forecasts suggest France's next heatwave is only days away.President Emmanuel Macron says criticism should not be the priority right now. "We will have to replant and rebuild a different kind of forest because we must adapt to the structural conditions of climate change," he said this week."The time for reviewing lessons learned will come," he insisted. "In the meantime, the country must remain united."Even so, the damage these fires have inflicted on the environment, hundreds of homes, tourism, local businesses and air quality has left the French public with a lot of questions.

schema.headline: Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame?

title: Syria court sentences Bashar al-Assad sentenced to death in absentia
description: A Syrian court has sentenced ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia, after convicting him of committing war crimes and crimes against hu
body: A Syrian court has sentenced ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia, after convicting him of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity during the country's civil war.It is the first conviction against Assad, who fled from Damascus to the Russian capital, Moscow, with his family after his regime was overthrown in December 2024, ending his family's five-decade grip on power.Assad's cousin and the former head of political security in southern Syria's Deraa province, Atef Najib, was also sentenced to death. He appeared wearing a striped prison uniform inside a cage in the courtroom as the judge read out his sentence.Deraa is widely seen as the birthplace of the uprising against Assad's rule.In March 2011, the detention and alleged torture of a group of teenagers accused of writing anti-government graffiti sparked protests in the city, which were met with a violent crackdown by security forces.That response helped ignite nationwide demonstrations that escalated into civil war in which hundreds of thousands of people were killed.Syria's interim government began trying officials associated with the Assad regime, which ruled the country for more than 50 years, earlier this year.Najib is one of the highest-ranking officials to be put on trial.He was convicted of crimes including murder, "the intentional killing of children under 15" and "torture leading to death".The court also sentenced six former military and security officials in absentia to death, including Bashar al-Assad's younger brother, Maher. He ran the army's elite Fourth Division and also fled to Moscow when the regime fell.The others convicted include former defence minister Fahd al-Freij.Outside the courthouse after the ruling, hundreds of people of all ages gathered holding pictures of their loved ones who were killed by the regime.Crowds were clapping and chanting, while cars drove by excitedly honking their horns.A group of men passed out flags."The joy is indescribable," one man told the BBC, hoisting up a photo of his late father. "God willing we will see Bashar al-Assad and all his aides hanging on the gallows."Another woman told the BBC everyone is feeling a mix of "victory and liberation.""The voices of the victims are finally heard. Justice has been achieved!" she exclaimed.Nouha al-Masri, a prosecutor in the case, lost her brother during the March 2011 crackdown and massacre at al-Omari Square in Deraa."We have been waiting for 15 years to reclaim even a small part of our rights, for all those who have spilled our blood, committed crimes, violated our rights, killed, and tortured us," Masri - now a member of the prosecution team, told the BBC."Our demand is that this not be the end of the trials... In the new Syria, there will be no impunity from this day forward."It remains unclear whether Syria's new authorities will be able to secure Bashar and Maher al-Assad's extraditions from Moscow.It is not the first move against Assad by Syria's new leadership.An arrest warrant was issued against him last December on charges of murder and torture.He left for Russia as forces under Ahmed al-Sharaa - now Syria's president - swept to power in a rapid, 11-day campaign that brought down the Assad dynasty.Since then, the new government has detained numerous former officials and security personnel, though most senior figures from the old regime, including Assad himself, remain out of reach in Russia.Attempts by Syrian opposition figures to pursue Assad through courts in Western countries during the final years of his rule did not lead to any convictions.Assad came to power in 2000 after the death of his father. The second son of Hafez al-Assad, he was not destined to be Syria's ruler until his brother, Basil, died in a car crash in 1994.Part of the Alawite minority, he continued to favour their dominance in many roles in the military, security and intelligence agencies. Much of his rule was defined by the civil war.Additional reporting by Lana Antaki in Damascus and Leen Alsaadi, BBC Arabic in Deraa.

schema.headline: Syria court sentences Bashar al-Assad sentenced to death in absentia

title: Trump hid in catering truck in secret plane swap over Iran threat, reports say
description: Figure caption, Watch: President Trump secretly switches planes to avoid Iran threatByJessica RawnsleyUpdated 2 hours agoDonald Trump secretly swapped
body: Figure caption, Watch: President Trump secretly switches planes to avoid Iran threatByJessica RawnsleyUpdated 2 hours agoDonald Trump secretly swapped planes as he left a Nato summit in Turkey last month, as part of an elaborate ruse in response to a possible Iranian threat, US media report.The US president boarded Air Force One in view of television cameras before being  transported to a military aircraft with the help of a catering truck, the Washington Post said. Journalists and some White House staff on board did not know he had been smuggled out. Officials told the BBC's US partner CBS News that the US had detected a credible Iranian threat to fire a missile at the plane. The White House has not confirmed the secret switch.Trump had earlier said he was Iran's "number one target" during the summit in Ankara. The clandestine manoeuvre came a day after the US renewed military strikes on Iran following a breakdown of negotiations between Washington and Tehran to end the war.Trump had arrived in Turkey aboard a newer Boeing 747-8 donated by Qatar, but announced that he would leave on the old Air Force One "for old time's sake".On 8 July, footage showed him boarding the presidential jet at Ankara airport. But according to the Washington Post, he was then secretly taken to a smaller C-32A military aircraft - a modified Boeing 757 often used by the vice-president - via a catering truck which had been elevated to plane level on the opposite side to where he had boarded.Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth boarded the C-32A separately using external stairs in an effort to make the flight appear normal, according to the newspaper.Journalists and some White House staff boarded Air Force One and were reportedly told to close their window shades. They were unaware the president was no longer on board.A pool producer who was on the plane said one unusual moment on the flight was the request that members of the press keep the shades down.  A photographer briefly opened one and was quickly told to close it and that it was a request from the Secret Service, which guards the president. The producer, in a report from the White House Correspondents Association provided on Tuesday, also noted there appeared to have been two catering trucks at both the front and back of the plane when the press arrived, and their van had been too far back in the motorcade at the airport be able to take a photo of the president boarding.Technically "Air Force One" is the call sign for any aircraft carrying the US president. But on this occasion, the C-32A used the call sign "Reach 18", while the aircraft carrying the journalists continued to use "AF1" in order to keep up the ruse.Trump then flew to the UK en route to the US, where he reboarded the old Air Force One and was seen descending from the aircraft after it landed at RAF Mildenhall. It is unclear how he moved from the C-32A back to the legacy jet. Image source, ReutersImage caption, He then boarded the Qatar-gifted jet to fly from the UK to the USThe president then transferred to the new Qatari-donated Air Force One to travel back to Washington. During that flight, Trump spoke to reporters on board where he noted the threats posed by Iran but did not mention the earlier plane swap.Asked why reporters had been told to lower the window shades on the plane from Turkey, Trump said: "Because you're probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleazebags we have to deal with."He said he had a "threat all the time" on his life, and that he is "number one" on Iran's "list"."But if I go, you go, right?", he said, adding: "Perhaps someday you want to change professions."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Trump spoke about the threat to him from Iran after boarding the presidential jet given to him by QatarWhite House communications director Steven Cheung did not directly confirm or deny the reports, but said the new Air Force One was a "state-of-the-art aircraft" fitted with security measures to protect the president and his staff.US intelligence had previously warned of a specific threat of an attack on Trump or his aircraft, according to earlier reporting by CBS News.The New York Times previously reported on security concerns regarding the Qatari-gifted jet, including that the Secret Service had urged Trump to switch planes on his return from the Nato summit.Several of the publication's journalists were summoned to testify under oath in response. The Justice Department subsequently told the BBC that it was investigating illegal leaks.The US has spent months retrofitting the $400m Boeing 747-8 to prepare it for the president. Older Air Force One planes have laser technology to blind incoming missiles, sources have told CBS News. It is unclear what systems the Qatari jet has."The new Air Force One is perfectly safe for the president's travels, but will receive additional upgrades and enhancements in the fall which will take approximately one month to complete," White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said in a statement to CBS News.

schema.headline: Trump hid in catering truck in secret plane swap over Iran threat, reports say

title: Russia using North Korean missiles to strike Ukraine, Zelensky says
description: Ukraine and Russia have continued striking each other overnight, with President Volodymyr Zelensky accusing Moscow of using North Korean missiles.Ukra
body: Ukraine and Russia have continued striking each other overnight, with President Volodymyr Zelensky accusing Moscow of using North Korean missiles.Ukraine said strikes on the southern city of Zaporizhzhia - which killed seven people and injured at least 24 - involved ballistic missiles from Russia's ally.In Voronezh, western Russia, warehouses of the biggest online retailer Wildberries were hit by Ukraine. The company, known as Russia's Amazon, has been repeatedly targeted in recent weeks.The attacks come a day after at least 13 people were killed, including one child, in Ukrainian drone strikes on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, more than 1,100 km (680 miles) from the Ukrainian border.In a video address on Monday evening, Zelensky said "for the first time" Russia "cannot wage war without reinforcements from North Korea"."The more North Korean strikes there are here in Ukraine, in Europe, the more their missiles and soldiers are used, the more they correct their shortcomings and blind spots", Zelensky said, adding that this poses a danger to the rest of the world.He has not presented any evidence to back up his comments. It is not the first time Zelensky as well as other senior Ukrainian and Western officials have accused Russia of receiving military assistance from North Korea.Ukraine's military has said that says dozens of North Korean missiles have been fired by Russia into its territory since Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022.The Ukrainian president warned over the weekend that as many as 50,000 North Korean soldiers were being sent to fight with Russian forces. Some 11,000 North Korean soldiers were deployed to help Moscow push Ukrainian troops out of the western Russian region of Kursk following their cross-border incursion in August 2024.In January 2025, Western officials told the BBC that North Korean troops had suffered nearly 40% casualties in the fighting there in just three months.In his Monday's address, Zelensky also hailed a successful air strike on a Russian petrochemical plant in western Siberia on Monday as a "very significant achievement" by the Ukrainian military.He promised "more Ukrainian deep strikes, which should demonstrate to Russia and the Russians that peace is necessary".Zaporizhzhia regional head Ivan Fedorov posted photos of vehicles and buildings on fire, saying Moscow had struck the city using missiles and guided bombs.All seven casualties were employees of Ukraine's Metinvest metallurgical plant, which later halted all its operations.One person was injured in strikes on the capital Kyiv, where air raid sirens sounded twice during the night. Explosions could be heard on the outskirts of the capital, triggering fires.Local officials later said a children's hospital was damaged - but there were no injuries as staff and patients were sheltering. Two women have been injured in a Russian drone strike on the north-eastern Ukrainian city of Sumy, according to regional head Serhii Kryvosheienko.He later said that one person was killed when Russia attacked the city with gliding bombs in the afternoon.Meanwhile, strikes on substations in Kherson and Kharkiv resulted in power outages.Ukrainian officials say Russia fired 120 drones overnight and a range of different missiles, but for the first time they have not given a number of missiles fired or intercepted.It follows an Air Force statement on Monday urging the media not to write "sensationalised headlines" or "spread pessimism" about the shortage of air defence interceptors.Separately, there have been reports of a fire and explosions at a logistics centre of Wildberries in the Voronezh region.Wildberries has not yet confirmed the attack, but said that its facilities in the region, which borders Ukraine, have been evacuated.In July, Ukrainian drone attacks on several retail warehouses belonging to Wildberries disrupted the operations of a large number of small and medium-sized Russian businesses.Kyiv said at the time it was targeting logistics hubs used by Russians to buy military equipment, and disrupting supplies to the Russian army.The attack on Tatarstan this week was one of the deadliest single attacks on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.At least 75 people were injured in the strikes, with Ukraine's Armed Forces saying it had hit the city's Tanevo oil refinery.Verified images on social media showed large plumes of smoke and flames rising into the sky in daytime, with air raid sirens howling in the background.The Uzbek consulate in Tatarstan said seven of those killed were citizens of Uzbekistan.

schema.headline: Russia using North Korean missiles to strike Ukraine, Zelensky says

title: Australia PM Anthony Albanese under fire for remarks over Sanae Takaichi's melon gift
description: Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is under fire for comments he made about two melons gifted to him by his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaic
body: Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is under fire for comments he made about two melons gifted to him by his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi, after a former Japanese envoy called it an insult.During an appearance on the Bush Deep podcast, Albanese gestured near his chest while referring to the crown melons, calling them "pretty strange" gifts that "ended up being quite good".That episode, which aired in July, had already landed the PM in hot water because of "inappropriate" comments he made about popstar Kylie Minogue.Opposition leaders are now demanding he apologise to Takaichi, but Albanese's position is that it was the host who made the joke, not him, the BBC understands.While discussing the melons Takaichi's team had presented to Albanese during her visit to Australia in May, the host of Bush Deep, comedian Nikki Osborne, quipped: "She brought two... She just came in looking like Pamela Anderson.""She brought two, and they are beautiful," Albanese responded.The exchange, which drew relatively little interest when the episode aired, has resurfaced after Tokyo's former ambassador to Canberra Shingo Yamagami labelled Albanese's comments a "sexist joke" and said they "betrayed the close bond" between Japan and Australia."The last thing [Takaichi] expected was to be so casually mocked by the trusted leader of Japan's special strategic partner," he wrote in an opinion piece published by The Australian on Monday.Crown melons are the "most prized fruit" in Japan and "treasured as something special", Yamagami added, noting that a single melon costs more than 30,000 yen ($188)."So, prime minister, please enjoy Japan's sweet and juicy melons without thinking about a woman's anatomy, and instead focus on what our two countries must do together," he said.During his two-year stint in Australia, Yamagami had a notably frosty relationship with some members of Albanese's Labor Party over disagreements regarding China.An opposition MP asked Albanese on Tuesday if he would apologise for the "foul-mouthed, classless comments about women", to which the prime minister said he "rejected the assertion of the question".He went on: "Australia and Japan have never been closer. My government has taken our special strategic partnership to new heights."Australia's opposition leader Angus Taylor on Monday also criticised the gaffe as "insulting", and demanded that Albanese make a personal apology.Several Labor ministers have jumped to Albanese's defence, saying the former envoy and the media have misinterpreted his comments.Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said the remarks "were not intended to be interpreted the way that our political opponents and some media outlets are reporting".Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek called it "a completely unnecessary interpretation of what the prime minister said". "I think people watching it for themselves can make their own minds up," Plibersek told Australia's Channel Seven.Plibersek had earlier defended Albanese's controversial remarks about Minogue as nothing more than a sign that he was a fan.The prime minister drew a wave of condemnation early last month after Osborne asked him on the podcast whether he would "shag, marry or date" Kylie Minogue, actress Nicole Kidman or entertainer Rhonda Burchmore, to which he replied "Kylie, clearly... all of the above".Albanese later issued a public apology, saying: "I apologise unequivocally for the comments".Osborne, who is best known for posting crude comedy sketches on YouTube, launched her podcast series earlier this year. Her podcast site describes her as a "wildly inappropriate journalist" who asks "questions no one else would dare".

schema.headline: Australia PM Anthony Albanese under fire for remarks over Sanae Takaichi's melon gift

title: Trump signs order to limit childhood vaccines and split MMR shots
description: US President Donald Trump has signed an order that calls for fewer childhood vaccines and also recommends splitting the mumps, measles and rubella (MM
body: US President Donald Trump has signed an order that calls for fewer childhood vaccines and also recommends splitting the mumps, measles and rubella (MMR) shots."Decades ago, children received only a small fraction of the vaccines required today," Trump said. "In those times, people were much healthier and of course the high rates of autism now observed did not exist."The president has long cast doubt on the safety of MMR vaccines, but multiple studies have found no connection between the shots and autism.Medical experts have criticised the new order and said it could reduce vaccination rates and expose children to harmful diseases.The order also recommends that the number of childhood vaccines drop to 11 from the existing 18 recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP).Trump's order serves as guidance, not a mandate, since shots required for school attendance are set at the state level, rather than by the federal government.The immunisations recommended for all children under the order are for measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus, and varicella or chicken pox."We're reducing them," Trump said. "It's not only that you're doing fewer vaccines, or jabs, as they say, but you're doing them in a series of visits to the doctor."The president suggested the MMR vaccine could be "quite lethal" if given at once. He compared it to pouring a bottle of soda into a child's body. According to the FDA, external, a single dose of MMR is 0.5ml.When a reporter asked for evidence of the "lethal" claim, Trump said: "What I've heard is that there are some people that say it is that way."According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), external, the MMR vaccine carries a very small risk of febrile seizures for young children. Those with health issues, including severe allegeric reactions or weakened immune systems, are advised to consult with healthcare providers before taking the shots.The agency says "most people who get MMR vaccine do not have any serious problems with it", and that getting the vaccine "is much safer than getting measles, mumps, or rubella".According to the CDC, there is "no published scientific evidence that shows any benefit in separating the combination MMR vaccine into three individual shots". Experts say that allowing time between jabs means children are more likely to contract diseases in the interim or that they are more likely to miss appointments if there are multiple shots.Dr William Schaffner of the Vanderbilt University School of Medicine in Nashville told the BBC the increased number of visits would be harder for parents and providers to track and would add to the expense without any scientific benefit.Since taking office in 2025, Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) Robert F Kennedy Jr has sought to change and loosen vaccine regulations. During a tense 20-minute interview on CNN last week, Kennedy insisted he had "never questioned the efficacy of the MMR vaccine".He said the proposed changes were meant to give parents choice, not prohibit access to childhood vaccines.Trump administration officials have said the order means children in the US would receive much less than the 72 shots recommended under the previous vaccine schedule, a figure that assumes annual flu and Covid-19 doses.Dr Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said Trump's executive order was "dangerous" and not based on "gold-standard science"."Delaying or skipping shots is risky, especially as measles continues to spread and children go back to school," Racine said. Republican Senator Bill Cassidy, who was the deciding vote in the Senate to confirm Kennedy as health secretary, also admonished Trump's executive order on Monday, labelling it "wrong"."The President does not have the expertise to make these changes," Cassidy, a physician, wrote on X. "Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism."Experts fear that if parents refrain from getting their children vaccinated as a result of the discredited idea that childhood vaccines are linked to autism, it risks the re-emergence of diseases like measles.Multiple studies have found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism. A recent high-quality study from Denmark in 2019 looked at 657,461 children and concluded that the data did not support the MMR vaccine causing or triggering autism.On its website, the CDC recommends that two doses of the combined MMR vaccine be given to children, starting with the first dose at 12-15 months and the second between the ages of four and six.How often and how many vaccines children in the US receive is based on the times when vaccines will work best with their immune systems and when they are most vulnerable to certain diseases, according to the AAP.There is no medical reason to delay or skip recommended immunisations, the AAP says.Trump's order also calls for the development of alternatives to aluminium in vaccines, and to test if those alternatives are safer and more effective.But the AAP, external says studies have found no significant health risks associated with the tiny amounts of aluminium salts in vaccines.Small amounts of aluminium salts - which are found naturally in soil, water and foods - have been used in some vaccines for decades in order to boost the body's immune response. That means lesser quantities of the vaccine and fewer doses are needed, according to AAP.

schema.headline: Trump signs order to limit childhood vaccines and split MMR shots

title: Luigi Mangione appears in court as questions in case remain ahead of murder trial
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByKayla EpsteinUpdated 37 minutes agoThe judge overseeing the state trial of Luigi Mangione, the man accused of killing Unit
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByKayla EpsteinUpdated 37 minutes agoThe judge overseeing the state trial of Luigi Mangione, the man accused of killing UnitedHealthcare chief executive Brian Thompson, has laid down the ground rules for court public and media access to the high-profile case. Mangione returned to court on Tuesday ahead of his murder trial, which begins next month in New York.The case has attracted national attention, and has also created an online frenzy, with both his backers - many of whom see Mangione as a symbol of the backlash against US healthcare costs - and his critics analysing everything from his intentions to his appearance. The spectacle is likely to intensify when jury selection for the trial begins on 8 September. Mangione, if found guilty, could face decades behind bars. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges, including second-degree murder and weapons-related offences. He faces a separate federal trial next year, in which he has also pleaded not guilty.Much of what is expected at the state trial – the prosecutor's case, Mangione's defence, and obstacles both parties face – were previewed in months of court filings and arguments, but some questions remain unanswered. Will the prosecution win battle over evidence?One of the most crucial elements of the Mangione case was decided earlier this summer, after a multi-day hearing in December where the judge weighed which evidence prosecutors could present during trial.Mangione's team mounted an aggressive bid to exclude evidence recovered from his Pennsylvania arrest. It alleged that state police improperly seized and searched Mangione's possessions, and did not properly advise him of his constitutional rights before questioning him.The defence succeeded in excluding some items, including a gun magazine, cell phone, passport, wallet and computer chip found in Mangione's backpack.But Judge Gregory Carro allowed at trial a gun and notebook with Mangione's purported writings, viewed as vital to the prosecution. Prosecutors have unveiled surveillance footage showing the moment Thompson was shot from behind by a hooded individual. They also used footage to piece together Mangione's alleged movements after the shooting, and ballistics and fingerprint evidence they claim bolsters their case. What might Mangione's defence look like?As trial approaches, Mangione's team has yet to unveil its full strategy. So far, his lawyers have not offered a robust alternative theory to the one prosecutors have put forth. "We do not have, like in 'The Fugitive,' the idea of the one-armed man who's the real killer," said former federal prosecutor Mitchell Epner, referencing a 1993 thriller about a man wrongly convicted of killing his wife.Earlier this summer, Mangione's lawyers proposed, then quickly withdrew, an  "extreme emotional disturbance" argument. In such a defence, New York law requires lawyers to show a defendant "acted under the influence of extreme emotional disturbance for which there was a reasonable explanation or excuse". Extreme emotional disturbance would allow the jury to consider the less severe charge of manslaughter, rather than second-degree murder. But jurors would have to be convinced of the accused's state of mind at the time.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Mangione's defence team leave court. Pictured from left to right: Marc Agnifilo, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, and Jacob Kaplan.Some experts wondered if Mangione would argue a full insanity plea - different from emotional disturbance, but his lawyers have not proposed it."Short of being delusional, or having no understanding of the nature of what one is doing, an insanity defence is not likely to be successful," said Cheryl Bader, who leads the Criminal Defence Clinic at the Fordham University School of Law.Mangione's team did not immediately respond to a request for comment.As in every US criminal trial, the burden rests on the prosecution to prove its case to the jury beyond a reasonable doubt, a high legal bar."The more his case is about the question of who killed the victim, the easier it is for the prosecution," said Epner. Epner cited other themes, including healthcare in America, as potential narrative threads that could sway a jury in Mangione's favour."The more it's about the other peripheral issues, the harder it is for the prosecution," he said.Who will be able to watch?In recent weeks, Mangione's lawyers and prosecutors have traded terse court filings debating just how much access the public will have to the trial. The trial is expected to generate coverage across traditional outlets, social media, and streaming platforms. Mangione's supporters have demanded more transparency, and frequently post and broadcast from outside court.On Tuesday, Carro said the court would open an overflow room during the trial, which will allow more members of the public and press to attend in person.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Public spectators leave Mangione's hearing, one of them wearing a shirt that demands officials "open the courtroom".In earlier court filings, Mangione's lawyers had questioned the court's press procedures, and why the court had not yet established an overflow room to meet public demand. They also implied – and later walked back – that prosecutors were influencing the court's media policies, which the Manhattan District Attorney's office denied.Carro took to the bench to rebuke Mangione's attorneys for their filings, saying "any suggestion the district is involved is simply incorrect". He also chastised prosecutors for raising security concerns about an overflow room, telling them it was not the court's "first rodeo" with blockbuster cases.While the public can be admitted to court in New York, space is often limited at high-profile trials.The court and its press office "remain firmly committed to providing the greatest possible access for both the media and the public", spokesman Al Baker said, adding that the court is "evaluating the complex logistical and safety considerations involved".

schema.headline: Luigi Mangione appears in court as questions in case remain ahead of murder trial

title: The lonely Chinese men being conned by fake brides
description: Figure caption, Watch: Chinese man targeted by 'flash wedding' scamsByLaura BickerChina correspondentReporting fromBeijing and GuiyangAt 37, Wang Zhua
body: Figure caption, Watch: Chinese man targeted by 'flash wedding' scamsByLaura BickerChina correspondentReporting fromBeijing and GuiyangAt 37, Wang Zhuang had almost given up hope of finding a wife, until he saw the glossy matchmaking adverts.They promised he wouldn't have to waste years on building a relationship that had no future. They offered to introduce him to a demure, devoted woman."The matchmakers said that girls from Guizhou are frugal," Wang says. "They told me they are good at running a household, able to do housework, and their families are very poor, so after marrying into your family, they would settle down and live a life with you."So Wang travelled to Guiyang, a city in the southwestern province of Guizhou, in the hope of finding his soulmate.He thought he had, when he was matched with a woman who seemed to tick every box. They had only met a few times before they married.Then, almost as quickly as his new life had begun, it was over."My whole family has been thrown into chaos," he says, shaking his head.He is still picking up the pieces more than a year after he discovered that everything he had been told by his wife was a lie.She was a former karaoke hostess who'd been married three times, had three children, a serious sexually transmitted disease and was deeply in debt. She had even lied about her age.He is fighting for a divorce and cannot return home to his old life - at least until he can recoup some of his life savings, which he says he paid to the agency within hours of being introduced to several potential matches."My parents blame me. I have insomnia and anxiety. I can't focus on work."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Chinese brides are in huge demand because of a steep gender imbalanceWang's story is an extreme symptom of a demographic crisis that has long been in the making in China.For decades, China's Communist Party decreed that couples could have only one child. They reversed course in January 2016 but by then the "one-child" policy, coupled with a preference for boys, had produced a shrinking pool of women and a stark gender imbalance.There are now 30 million more men than women in China – that's more than the male population of the UK, or the entire population of Australia.This has left men like Wang, who are in their late 30s and who live in smaller cities or far-flung, rural areas, with few options. Women in these places can afford to be choosy as they know they are in demand."The requirements for men are very high in my city. You need to have a car, a house and your family should preferably run a business," he says.Many families also demand a high "bride price", a longstanding Chinese custom where the groom's family gives money to the bride. In parts of China, where men far outnumber women, this has become a significant financial burden.Hence the appeal of matchmaking agencies like the ones in Guizhou, which are proposing a one-stop, quick solution - or "flash marriages".Matchmaking agencies are hardly new in China, but many seem to be finding vulnerable targets in men who are struggling to find partners as they grow older.So much so that state media recently reported that the industry had seen "rapid growth" which  had "bred illegal practices and chaos".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The "flash marriage" market is now on Beijing's radarIt's hard to determine the scale of such fraud across China but it has grown enough to draw the attention of Chinese officials. Between January 2024 and March 2025, prosecutors handled cases involving 1,546 individuals for crimes related to the matchmaking industry.This month, five separate authorities jointly launched a nationwide crackdown on the matchmaking industry after the issue generated "widespread public concern".In one case, a matchmaking agency reportedly used karaoke waitresses as bait to defraud 128 victims of more than 2.5 million yuan (£274,000, $371,000)."I think the government could introduce industry-specific regulations targeting flash marriage scams," Fan Binghe, from the Nanjing Office of the Beijing Jingshi law firm, told the BBC.Although Guiyang has become synonymous with this booming "flash marriage" market, there is little to suggest it is a romantic hub.The agency offices sit in a dense warren of buildings above a shopping precinct, where vendors sell local fruit and workers queue for takeaway sour soup rice noodles.Wang, however, was convinced he could trust them after the company told him they would do a full background check and that he would be entitled to compensation if he was the victim of fraud.So he paid up and the introductions began.Image caption, Wang was drawn to Guiyang by the promise of a demure spouse He met seven women in various "blind date" rooms over a few days while being carefully supervised by agency staff. He asked questions about where they came from, if they'd been married before and if they had any kids.He set his heart on the eighth woman he met. He was hoping to meet someone who hadn't been married before, with no children and who was just a little younger than him."She also dressed very simply," he recalls. "She looked introverted and honest."They met four or five times for just eight to 10 minutes each time. He says they had been under strict instructions not to exchange phone numbers or any details on private messages, or they would be fined.After two or three days he decided she was the one and he agreed to pay her a substantial bride price. "I spent more than 300,000 yuan [$44,000]," he says, with a pile of well-thumbed legal papers in hand to prove it."If you include the wedding banquet and everything else, I spent around 400,000 to 500,000 yuan."The whole process was documented by the matchmaking agency in a series of glossy photos, which they also use to advertise their services on Chinese social media. In the video the couple are holding hands on a red carpet and smiling while romantic music plays in the background.Image caption, Wang with his ex-wife in a photo taken soon after their wedding  Just months into the marriage, debt collectors started calling, alleging she owed them money.Wang grew suspicious and wanted to know what else she had kept hidden. He checked her phone and found details of her former life, her birth certificate and former marriage documents.When he confronted her, she offered him a divorce, but refused to return a single penny of the bride price.He says he tried to hunt down the agency responsible for his marriage, but when he returned to their offices, they had packed up and disappeared.From his rented flat in Guiyang, just across from the main district which houses most of these agencies, Wang now spends his time making social media videos trying to warn other men about what can go wrong.In Guiyang, it is difficult to find an agency where the staff is willing to talk. One agency boss agreed to talk to us in their offices – although his business partner later asked us to leave.Inside there was a red carpet littered with fake petals ready for a proposal. He told us a couple had pledged to marry just hours before we arrived."There's a huge market for flash marriages in China. It only really emerged over the last two or three years," he told us.The agencies claim families here did not strictly adhere to the one-child policy, which means the area has a larger pool of women. "Even if a family had two or three daughters, they would keep trying for a son," one of them told the BBC.They say they are now trying to match these women with men from central provinces – like Wang who lives in Hebei – who are relatively wealthy but have few women around them."Our clients are free to choose whoever they like. The purpose of our business is to help people find someone they genuinely want to be with."One of the advertisements assures their prospective clients that "Three days with the right introduction can beat three years of dating".Image caption, It was in a room like this where Wang met his brideWang now spends his time trying to help other victims of similar spiels.His rented flat is full of men who are either searching for the owners of the agency who scammed them, or are trying to recoup their losses from their wives who ran off after only a few weeks of marriage.On a fold-up bed by the window, 59-year-old Xu Rulin from Jiangxi province pulls his carefully collated evidence out of a red plastic shopping bag.He spent nearly 500,000 yuan trying to find his son a wife through a "flash marriage" agency.Together they travelled to Guiyang - more than 1,000km away - and his son wed just seven days after he first met his bride in a "blind date" room.Xu says after the marriage was registered, she demanded they buy her an iPhone and transfer around 20,000 yuan to help her with her business. She also asked for 120,000 yuan for a wedding dress and jewellery, he claims."All I wanted was for her to genuinely settle down and live with us," he told us. "She said she wanted a house and I agreed to buy one for them. It was all agreed."But he says she ran away after living with them for less than two weeks. She has been detained by the police, and the couple have been able to get divorced.He says the owners of the matchmaking company were also arrested in January this year, but he is still in Guiyang trying to recover some of the losses.Image caption, The bride Xu Rulin spent a fortune finding for his son ran away within two weeksThe agency manager the BBC spoke to admitted there were no formal background checks on their clients."The women are introduced by local matchmakers who already know them very well. They know their family background because they're often from the same village. The male's matchmaker also usually knows the man very well."They would not say how much their services cost because that information was "confidential".He did say that if the information provided by either side is not truthful, then the client is entitled to get their money back."I'd say more than 90% of what our clients tell us here is true," he claimed."We have a saying here in China. One rotten mouse dropping spoils the whole pot of soup. That's exactly what it's like. We regularly attend meetings with the local police. If a matchmaking agency is found to be involved in marriage fraud, it will be held legally responsible."Image caption, This matchmaker says most people in the industry are genuineThis brings little comfort for those who have lost whatever money they had saved."I never imagined that with the agency charging such a high service fee, a local matchmaker in her hometown checking her background and the company offering so many guarantees, that the women's information would turn out to be completely fake," Wang says.He is almost resigned now to his losses. And he blames himself for falling for the scam: "Only women with problems would agree to these kind of flash marriages."He has kneeled at the police offices in Guiyang pleading for them to help him get his money back and he has even travelled to Beijing to urge the authorities to do more to combat this type of crime.These cases are difficult to prosecute, says Fan Binghe, the lawyer who has handled many.For one, Chinese law has no specific criminal offence which covers this kind of marriage fraud, and so to bring criminal charges, a victim has to establish that the aim of their spouse was always to take their money."In cases I've handled, suspects often argue that they genuinely intended to marry and live a good life but realised they were incompatible, had conflicts, and decided to end the relationship," he says."In situations like that, the line becomes blurred. Relationship issues are difficult to disprove."Image caption, Wang's apartment has turned into a refuge for scammed menEven harder is getting money back from sham matchmaking agencies which often shut up shop as soon as they have made enough cash.Wang has managed to get some money back, but not all."After going through something like this, I don't even know if I can still get married. It was already hard for me to find someone. And now I've spent so much money. I won't consider it now."Wang's life, and the life of the men in the apartment, all appear to be in limbo."It has taken almost two years, and even now I still don't know when I can divorce her," he says, surrounded by his legal paperwork."I don't know when this will be resolved, so I can restart a normal life. It feels endless."

schema.headline: The lonely Chinese men being conned by fake brides

title: The transgender controversy surrounding the WNBA
description: Last month, Cunningham, one of the league's most high-profile players, gave an interview to ESPN, external in which the conversation turned to the top
body: Last month, Cunningham, one of the league's most high-profile players, gave an interview to ESPN, external in which the conversation turned to the topic of "protecting" women's sports.The Indiana Fever guard said she had received criticism from people who believed she "hated" transgender people, something she denied.She said she wanted to "extend love" to everyone, but added: "I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."She later doubled down on her comments, saying it was "common sense", external to bar transgender athletes from competing in women's sports.Her words quickly moved beyond basketball and into a wider political debate in the United States.President Donald Trump expressed his support for Cunningham, while vice-president JD Vance said she was "inspiring".Though the 29-year-old later said she is "not a very political person", her remarks have followed her around the country. Competing rallies from critics and supporters were organised at Indiana's games, along with small-scale protests.The scale of the debate in the media, online and in politics was striking given no openly transgender woman is due to play, or has ever played, in the WNBA.The WNBA operates under a collective bargaining agreement (CBA), a deal negotiated between the league and its players association (WNBPA), setting rules on matters including player salary caps, revenue sharing, benefits and overall league operations.On player eligibility, the CBA states: "Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA."The WNBA has yet to comment publicly on the row since Cunningham's comments but league commissioner Cathy Engelbert reportedly sent a memo to teams last week in which she said the matter would be discussed at an upcoming pre-arranged meeting with team presidents.In the memo, seen by the Associated Press, external, Engelbert said the league would "always approach this topic thoughtfully, respectfully, and in alignment with the longstanding values of our league".She added: "Our player eligibility rules, unlike the eligibility rules of some other leagues and governing bodies, are collectively bargained. Preserving the integrity of our game and ensuring fair competition will always remain among the league's highest priorities."However, the lack of detail in the league's eligibility criteria has been brought to light by Kanter Freedom, who finished his playing career with the Boston Celtics in 2022."If simply declaring who you are is all that's required, then I meet every single requirement necessary to compete in the WNBA," he wrote on Instagram, external.Kanter Freedom, who has previously spoken out about human rights violations in China and Turkey, among other issues, added: "I know my presence on the court will stir up strong opinions. I am definitely not here to mock, make fun of, or disrespect any community or personal choices."I'm simply asking that the current rules be applied equally to everyone - the rules that represent the very values many WNBA players and coaches have publicly advocated for."A day after Kanter Freedom's 'announcement', Royce White - who made three appearances in the NBA as a player and is now a Republican Senate candidate - said he would also declare for the Draft, adding: "I identify as sometimes identifying as a woman for purpose of basketball."Whether the vagueness of the rules are by design to leave it open to transgender women or a sign of an oversight that genuinely needs tightening up is not clear.BBC Sport has contacted Cunningham's representatives, the WNBA and WNBPA for comment.Cunningham's comments have become a flashpoint inside a league which has a long history of player activism on issues including race, gender equality and LGBTQ+ rights.The players' association did not mention Cunningham by name when it eventually addressed the debate.In a statement the WNBPA denounced "hate abuse and demonisation of the transgender community" and reaffirmed its commitment to "justice, equity, diversity and inclusion".It called on fans to report abusive behaviour at games and added that it would continue to have "hard" conversations but it "will not be used as political pawns".There is strong feeling on both sides of the argument. Minnesota Lynx head coach and president Cheryl Reeve, who said: "I come from a space of inclusion."The narrative that I think is problematic is to suggest that transgender athletes are the biggest problem in women's sports."Reeve wore a "Trans Kids Belong" T-shirt before Minnesota played Indiana earlier this month and was seen speaking to Cunningham on court before the game.Cunningham later said the pair had exchanged their perspectives and that the conversation ended with "love and respect".Golden State Valkyries forward Gabby Williams said she would welcome a transgender athlete "on my team or against my team, any time".Last month, the WNBA suspended Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton from attending the team's next five home games after an exchange with two fans, who were sat courtside displaying signs thanking Cunningham for "speaking up for girls".Keaton reportedly confronted the teenage fans and admonished them during the game. The Storm have since apologised.As for Cunningham, the attention has increasingly become an unwelcome distraction.Having defended her original comments, she said recently that she now wanted the conversation to return to what was happening on court."I want to get back to basketball, it's always been about basketball" she said, arguing that the standard of play in the WNBA was being overshadowed by issues away from the game.But that may prove difficult, as pressure grows on the league to clarify exactly who is eligible to play.In recent years, many governing bodies in sport have amended their rules about the inclusion of transgender athletes at the elite level, moving more towards restrictions.Athletics, cycling and aquatics, for example, have implemented outright bans on transgender women taking part in women's events.In March, it was announced that the women's category of Olympic sports will be limited to biological females from the LA Olympic Games in 2028.The International Olympic Committee (IOC) says eligibility will be determined by a "once-in-a-lifetime" sex test, which would prevent transgender women and those with differences in sexual development (DSD) who have gone through male puberty from competing.In the United States, transgender women and girls are banned from competing in women's sports categories in schools, universities and the grassroots level.That was part of an executive order - titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" - signed by President Trump last year. It does not cover professional sport.

schema.headline: The transgender controversy surrounding the WNBA

title: Family's narrow escape before earthquake shakes home
description: A family captured video of the moment they fled their home during an earthquake in Colombia.Liliana Pérez Ocampo and her family escaped moments before
body: A family captured video of the moment they fled their home during an earthquake in Colombia.Liliana Pérez Ocampo and her family escaped moments before their home was rocked by a 7.4 magnitude quake on Monday."At first, we thought it was just a mild tremor like the ones that usually happen in Colombia, but when more than 30 seconds passed and everything was shaking harder, we realised it was an earthquake," the mother-of-four told the BBC World Service.Her family, including two young children at school, are safe."In the end, material things can be replaced," she said. "The most important thing is life, and we have that."With at least 169 people killed, this has been the strongest earthquake to hit Colombia in the 21st Century, according to the country's Geological Service.More on this story.

schema.headline: Family's narrow escape before earthquake shakes home

title: Watch: Manila river surface covered in tide of rubbish
description: Workers waded through a rubbish-filled river in Manila, collecting waste that washed in during days of heavy rain. The nine-day downpour, exacerbated
body: Workers waded through a rubbish-filled river in Manila, collecting waste that washed in during days of heavy rain. The nine-day downpour, exacerbated by tropical storms, was equivalent to more than a month's worth of rain in some areas. It resulted in school and government office closures across the main island of Luzon and flooding in the capital. Floods, landslides and accidents driven by the rains killed at least 16 people in the northern Philippines, rescuers said on Monday

title: What we know about Tupac murder suspect Duane 'Keffe D' Davis
description: The only suspect ever charged for the drive-by shooting that killed rap superstar Tupac Shakur on 7 September 1996 is Duane "Keffe D" Davis. The 63-ye
body: The only suspect ever charged for the drive-by shooting that killed rap superstar Tupac Shakur on 7 September 1996 is Duane "Keffe D" Davis. The 63-year-old former gang boss is due to stand trial in Las Vegas, where he is accused of murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang.He has pleaded not guilty.The BBC's journalist Anoushka Mutanda-Dougherty explains what we know about the suspect.Read more about the case here.

title: Russia releases former US Marine reported in poor health
description: Russia has released a former US Marine who was jailed in 2022 and was reportedly in extremely poor health.  Robert Gilman, from Massachusetts, was fre
body: Russia has released a former US Marine who was jailed in 2022 and was reportedly in extremely poor health.  Robert Gilman, from Massachusetts, was freed "from detention for humanitarian reasons" and flying on a US plane to Washington, DC, on Tuesday, according to Kirill Dmitriev, special envoy for Russian President Vladimir Putin.Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey posted on social media that Gilman had been "essentially catatonic" and battling a "severe case of pneumonia" before he was released.Gilman was 28 when he was arrested for kicking a police officer while drunk aboard a train to Moscow."Approximately 50 days ago, Robert was diagnosed with a dissociative stupor - a condition where he is non-responsive and unable to interact or eat," Markey said, adding that the details of Gilman's current condition were unknown.Reuters reported that multiple doctors were tending to Gilman as he returned to the  US and that a US official said "he seems to be in good shape".His family is awaiting his arrival at a military hospital in Texas, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner."I am so grateful to President Trump for saving my brother's life," Lexie Hudson, his sister said in a statement. "There is no other reason that Robert is alive today other than that President Trump heard about the case and took action."

schema.headline: Russia releases former US Marine reported in poor health

title: Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope
description: ByTiffanie TurnbullReporting fromDryandra, Western Australia"Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat.Obediently, we scan the ends
body: ByTiffanie TurnbullReporting fromDryandra, Western Australia"Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat.Obediently, we scan the ends and tops of logs, looking between low scrub and patches of vivid wildflowers for a flash of stripes or a dart of movement.Eluding us is the numbat, a rare Australian marsupial which could be the love-child of a chipmunk and an anteater.Numbats were once populous across the bottom half of the continent, but Dryandra Woodland – in the south-western corner of Australia – is one of the few places they remain.As we slowly roll along bush tracks, researchers explain how this annual trip helps plot the species' survival.Classified as endangered until this month, numbats have been bouncing back. This team's efforts have seen them scratched off the international red list of threatened species - a rare glimmer of hope in a country facing an extinction emergency.This part of Australia is the front line of that crisis: a last stand for many species driven to the brink by feral pests, disease, urban development, habitat destruction and climate change.Winging over our car at one point is the endangered Carnaby's cockatoo. On an island just off the coast is one of the last surviving pockets of the world's rarest marsupial, the Gilbert's potoroo. Diving in the sapphire waters around it is the increasingly scarce Australian sea lion.Image source, Sharon Jones/BBCImage caption, Dryandra Woodland is one of the few places you can still find wild numbatsAustralia has long been celebrated as a nature haven, home to some of the world's most unique plant and animal species. More than 80% cannot be found anywhere else.But it has arguably become the extinction capital of the world, losing roughly four species every decade - and the decline is only worsening.Dedicated volunteers and under-funded conservationists have been slowing the army of increasing threats, but experts fear that without urgent action and political courage, the biodiversity Australia says it loves is headed for a bloodbath."It's not even a case of imagining it, it's happening in front of our own eyes," Professor Euan Ritchie tells the BBC.The many threats driving extinctionImage source, Sharon Jones/BBCImage caption, Dr Tony Friend first started working at Dryandra in the 80sIf spotting a rare creature in the wild wasn't challenging enough, the numbat is a squirrel-sized camouflage connoisseur, explains Dr Tony Friend, the godfather of conservation in the state of Western Australia."They just slept in today," jokes Rob McLean, president of the Numbat Taskforce, a volunteer group which makes a lot of Tony's thinly-resourced work possible.For two weeks each spring, as the young start venturing from their burrows, this team drives a daily circuit and records every numbat spotted. They log GPS coordinates, measure the distance to the road, and use a complicated equation to estimate the density of the animals in these woods and, from that, broader population health.One person sits in concentrated silence at each window, another perched in the back of the pick-up truck, ducking for the occasional limb branching from trees which rise around us.Through the trunks, we get the occasional glimpse of the razed farmland which tightly fences this pocket of protected woodland. On the side of one trail is a machine which detects and sprays feral cats and foxes with poison, another reminder of the perils numbats face."This year's been a bit of a feast," Rob admits.For hours on end, we cruise around, seeing parrots, wallabies, a goanna and a couple of echidnas - but no numbats.Tony arrived at Dryandra back in the 80s to find a numbat population fewer than 50. Many of the culprits then were the same as those still driving extinctions across the nation today.Image source, Courtesy WA DBCAImage caption, Feral cats kill an estimated three billion animals in Australia each yearSwathes of critical habitat are being cleared for development or industries like farming, mining and timber. Leaving a trail of destruction in their wake are introduced pests: fire ants, cane toads, rabbits, foxes, feral cats.Invasive weeds like lantana are choking the Australian bush, chlamydia has sent koalas to the edge of existence across much of the country, while the skin-eating chytrid fungus has caused seven frog extinctions here and counting.The changing climate is creating unliveable conditions for some species, like native flying foxes which are dropping out of trees in their thousands due to extreme temperatures. For others it is eliminating their food or their homes.Climate change is also driving natural disasters which fry and drown both plants and animals with now frightening regularity. The infamous Black Summer bushfires of 2019-20, for example, killed an estimated three billion animals. The successive years of record-breaking flooding which followed were so widespread it's impossible to estimate the impact on wildlife.Image source, Sharon Jones/BBCImage caption, The Carnaby's black cockatoo is another species barely hanging on in south-western Australia Many species once abundant across the continent are now isolated to increasingly small and disjointed patches, each impact compounding and leaving them more vulnerable to the next.There are small, yet determined, efforts to slow the momentum of decline.As a young numbat scoffs his breakfast – custard with "termite sprinkles" – at Perth Zoo, a keeper explains how this stud's upcoming release at Dryandra will help boost genetic diversity."When you get that feedback: your babies have got babies, it's very satisfying," Vicki Power says.Breeding programmes like this have also made setting up additional populations of an array of threatened species possible.But many cannot survive in the true wild, where large-scale predator control remains an endless battle, and are instead sent to fenced nature reserves, themselves high-maintenance undertakings facing problems like in-breeding and overpopulation.Habitat protection or restoration projects have been ramping up, but they are not keeping pace with destruction, particularly in the most critical areas.Scientists are also trying to fight disease, though that's an expensive and laborious endeavour, which for most species buys only a little more time. Others are preserving genetic material in case we ever work out how to resurrect species from the dead.A hundred species lost - and countingScientists agree that we're living though the world's sixth mass extinction event, the first caused by humans. But Australia is at the front of this trend.It leads the world in mammal extinctions, and medals when it comes to the loss of other species classes too."Despite Australia being one of the wealthiest countries per capita in the world and having more than its fair share of world-leading scientists… we have a truly awful record of conserving species," Ritchie says."And things aren't getting better."The Australian government's official extinctions list sits at 67, but researchers are confident at least 100 plant and animal species have been lost forever.They suspect the true figure is far higher. The country is still discovering species which have already been wiped out.Though the rate of extinction in Australia has stayed stable, at around four per decade, the number of threatened species is still climbing quickly, and the deterioration of many is only gathering speed.This trajectory has some scary flow-on effects, experts warn. Australia's biodiversity "underpins everything", ecologist Jack Pascoe says.Think food production, tourism, construction – much of the economy. Potential scientific breakthroughs could be stymied: in medicine, agriculture and even climate change adaptation. And for First Nations Australians, the decline also threatens their culture."We think of ourselves as custodians of all life on Earth… so there's a much more personal and social feeling of loss that comes when these things are not doing well or we lose them forever," Pascoe, a man from the Yuin Aboriginal nation, says.Decades of failuresThough environment protection is a state responsibility, the federal government oversees matters of national importance.Labor took office in 2022, promising no new extinctions under its watch, and it has sought to make nature protection a defining feature of its second term."It's well understood that nature is facing many challenges in the world today, both here in Australia, and overseas… we are losing biodiversity at an alarming rate," Environment Minister Murray Watt told the BBC in a statement.His party has significantly increased Australia's emissions reduction efforts and massively boosted renewable energy projects. There is some praise for their work on drawing critically endangered mammals back from the brink. And the passage of revamped environment laws last year was heralded as the most significant reform in a generation.The country also has an ambitious goal to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.But there's limited optimism that this will be a real turning point.The new laws are only the scaffolding of change. The substance of it is still being worked out – in the form of National Environmental Standards (NES) and a federal watchdog to enforce them.And many in the sector say the problem is not so much the regulatory tools available, but rather the political will to use them.Successive governments have failed to adequately protect the environment over the past 30 years, Australia's longest serving environment minister tells the BBC.​​That includes his own administration. "We should have done more too," says Robert Hill, who lead the last major reforms in 1999 under John Howard's conservative coalition.Image source, Courtesy Perth ZooImage caption, Vicki Power and Tony Friend have spent decades trying to save the numbatMany of the challenges of his era still haunt leaders today.The nation's wealth has largely been built off the back of its natural resources – often at the expense of the environment. Those riches still underpin the economy and help fund government spending on essentials like healthcare and housing.Then there's the added pressure applied by industry and the competing interests of states - whose stake in regulatory controls blurs the lines of accountability and increases bureaucratic hurdles.These battles leave even the toughest environmental advocates within governments bruised.For example, the Albanese government last year rushed through laws protecting salmon farming after lobbying by Tasmanian state officials, silencing opposition from within and ignoring advice from its own department concerning the impact of the A$1.4bn (£733m; $989m) industry on the survival of the Maugean Skate, an endangered ray."The axe falls on the environmental outcome if there's the alternative of an economic one," Hill says."Even if [the federal government] does want to act, it's still got to have the political strength to turn its aspirations into reality."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Albanese government passed legislation to protect salmon farming after lobbying by Tasmanian state officialsThere is also a belief that greater regulation alone will achieve little.Too much conservation work currently relies on philanthropists' cash and devoted volunteers, those in the sector say, and much more languishes on the to-do list due to a lack of money.The federal government directly spends about A$700m on nature protection, a fraction of the A$33bn – or 1% of GDP – conservationists say it should be. That is an eyebrow-raising figure, people like Paul Elton concede, but one they argue is reasonable.According to his research – which the government disputes – more than A$26bn is still being spent on subsidies for things like mining, intensive agriculture or fuel despite Australia signing global pledges to wind them back."For every dollar the government is spending on positive biodiversity conservation action, there's A$26 being spent on subsidies that are causing harm to nature," he tells the BBC."That's a pretty stark imbalance."Minister Watt didn't directly respond to questions about conservationists' demands, but said: "We remain committed to long-term environmental recovery, in partnership with state and local governments, community and environmental groups."Though public sentiment is shifting, there's scepticism the government will prioritise the environment amid competing demands and compounding crises until voters force them to do so."The community will say to you, we should spend a lot of money on the environment. And then if you say, 'Well, what are you prepared to sacrifice to ensure that funding base?', then they're no longer interested," Hill says.In the face of so many challenges and what they see as little progress, advocates admit it's hard to hang on to hope."We know what the problems are. We know how to address them. We know when we spend money on the environment, it pays back many times over," Ritchie, a mammal ecologist, says."It's like being a doctor and seeing all these sick people in the community and you know how to fix them, but no one will let you do that."Image source, Sharon Jones/BBCImage caption, Volunteer 'Jacko' keeps watch from the back of the truckSmall wins, like the future of the numbat, keep them fighting.There are now around 3,000 nationwide, and in Dryandra numbers have increased ten-fold. The animal has recently been taken off the international endangered species list and is now classified as near-threatened.It takes five hours, but finally synchronised cries of excitement come from the driver's seat and the back of the pick-up truck. The cause of the commotion stands frozen and alert at the end of a hollowing log."It's not a competition," Rob says. Chuckling, he points at his rival spotter: "But I beat him by a second."The dam has broken. Over the next little while we see eight numbats, including two pairs of babies, blinking at us in the dusky light.This year's full count, Tony later tells me, is one of the best yet."But I remind people they're not out of the woods yet," Tony says.The relief at the numbat's revival is tempered by worry this will make it harder to access the funding and support needed to cement those gains.The woylie, or brush-tailed bettong, is a cautionary tale. It recovered slightly and was taken off the threatened list only to be added again a decade later, in a worse state."We can't walk away," Tony says, "and say 'no, they're fine,' you know?""It's got to be accepted that continued work is needed to keep that animal on the planet."AsiaAustraliaWildlifeWildlife conservation

schema.headline: Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope

title: Jackie the bald eagle dies after weeks of intensive care
description: Jackie, a bald eagle in California who became an online star, died on Monday after receiving weeks of veterinary treatment. Jackie was being cared for
body: Jackie, a bald eagle in California who became an online star, died on Monday after receiving weeks of veterinary treatment. Jackie was being cared for by Ojai Raptor Center, a wildlife rehabilitation organisation, after she was attacked by other eagles. The bird had underlying health issues that caused anaemia and weight loss. "Over the past several days, her condition continued to deteriorate despite intensive treatment and the combined efforts of our veterinary team and consulting specialists," Ojai Raptor Center said in a statement.  A livestream featuring the Big Bear Valley nest of Jackie and her partner, Shadow, has hundreds of thousands of subscribers.The Big Bear Eagle Nest Cam, run by the nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley in California, amassed a loyal following and Jackie was frequently spotted in the area since she hatched in the spring of 2012. Jackie and Shadow had been mates since 2018, the Friends of Big Bear Valley website said."Our team is heartbroken. It has been an extraordinary privilege to care for her," the Ojai Raptor Center said. "We know this news will be deeply felt by the many thousands of people around the world who have followed her journey, hoped alongside us, prayed for her, and supported the people caring for her."We are working closely with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife and will provide a more comprehensive statement including additional information on her treatments and test results." Jackie's remains have been transferred to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, the Ojai Raptor Center said.
